query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Applying ultrasonic vibration-assisted surface treatment to pre-exposure Q235 steel refines its near-surface grain structure, which in turn increases grain boundary density and promotes the rapid, uniform formation of a passive oxide film that suppresses corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 mild steel with a relatively coarse near-surface grain structure.
generation.intervention: Ultrasonic vibration-assisted surface treatment designed to induce severe plastic deformation and grain refinement near the surface.
generation.conditions: Samples are exposed to corrosive environments (e.g., saltwater or similar aggressive electrolyte) at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (e.g., around 300°C) for comparable durations.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined near-surface microstructure with increased grain boundary density resulting from the ultrasonic treatment.
generation.mechanism: The increased density of grain boundaries provides additional nucleation sites for oxidation, leading to the formation of a thicker, more uniform, and less defective passive film. This continuous film acts as an effective barrier against corrosive attack, thus reducing degradation rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated Q235 steel, the ultrasonically treated steel will exhibit a passive film that forms more rapidly and uniformly, resulting in lower corrosion current densities and enhanced polarization resistance under both room temperature and elevated temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated pre-exposure Q235 steel subjected to the same environmental conditions, expected to develop a less uniform and thinner passive film.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect may be limited if the ultrasonic treatment does not achieve sufficient grain refinement or if other corrosion mechanisms dominate at extremely high temperatures or long-term exposures.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of passivation improvement and the precise change in corrosion rates are not defined without experimental measurement; variability in treatment uniformity and environmental parameters could also influence the outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set undergoing ultrasonic vibration-assisted surface treatment and one control set with no treatment. Expose both sets to identical harsh corrosive environments at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (around 300°C) for predetermined time intervals. Ensure all other variables (e.g., sample dimensions, exposure time, electrolyte composition) are held constant.
measurements: Electrochemical measurements such as potentiodynamic polarization to assess corrosion current densities and polarization resistance.
Microscopic characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM) to evaluate passive film thickness, continuity, and defect density on the treated versus control surfaces.
Surface analysis (e.g., XPS) to characterize the composition and quality of the passive film.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrasonically treated Q235 steel does not display a statistically significant (e.g., >20% improvement) decrease in corrosion current density and increase in passive film uniformity/thickness relative to the control group under both temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that grain refinement via ultrasonic treatment improves passivation and suppresses corrosion is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The difference between the Ecorr and Epass values acts as an indicator for assessing an alloy’s passivation capability. Table 3 shows that the CR75 had the lowest Ecorr–Epass value (0.27 V), indicating that the alloy can quickly undergo passivation after corrosion. The high passivation ability of CR75 is attributed to its ultrafine grain size. After grain refinement treatment, the increase in the grain boundary density and dislocation density can reduce the surface work function and promote the formation of thicker and less defective passivation films [,]. In addition, more grain boundaries can provide more nucleation sites for oxidation in the passivation layer [,].

In the process of UB, the rolling head impacts the coating surface under the co-action of ultrasonic vibration and static pressure, leading to the severe plastic deformation of the coating surface, accompanied by plastic deformations such as crystal plane slip, twinning, and grain boundary migration, the formation of high-density dislocation tangles and dislocation walls, as well as the emergence of grain in a streamlined structure []. As a result, the processing quality of the alloy surface is improved with residual compressive stress, and the refined gradient structures are formed in the surface layer. Furthermore, the FeCoNiCr and CoCrNi MEAs have a single FCC structure with more slip systems than BCC and HCP, which is easier to slide to form a streamlined structure in the deformation process [,].

reading.lever: Apply ultrasonic vibration-assisted surface treatment to refine Q235 steel’s near-surface grain structure for enhanced, uniform passivation.
reading.why: Prior evidence indicates that increased grain boundary density improves passive film formation, a mechanism not yet applied to pre-exposed Q235 steel.
